archetypes.pitch: A relentless red swarm where dying Goblins are a resource, not a loss. Skirk Prospector sacrifices them for mana and Pashalik Mons turns each death into damage, while Siege-Gang Commander and Sulfuric Vortex push the last points through. Pick this if you love flooding the board and attacking without mercy.
archetypes.rationale: Pashalik Mons turns every Goblin death into damage and Skirk Prospector turns them into mana; Dralnu's Crusade ("All Goblins are black and are Zombies") lets Deadapult ("Sacrifice a Zombie: ...deals 2 damage") eat any Goblin, while Urza's Incubator and Cryptic Gateway cheat expensive Goblins like Siege-Gang Commander into play; Sulfuric Vortex is the cross-tag reach finisher that also shuts off opposing lifegain.

archetypes.pitch: A grindy black deck that feeds its own creatures into a value machine. Yawgmoth, Thran Physician draws cards and shrinks blockers while Oversold Cemetery keeps handing your fodder back, so you win the long attrition war. For players who enjoy squeezing advantage out of every death.
archetypes.rationale: Yawgmoth converts spare bodies into cards plus -1/-1 removal while Oversold Cemetery ("if you have four or more creature cards in your graveyard... return target creature card... to your hand") rebuys the fodder; cross-tag: Spinal Embrace steals a blocker you can feed to Phyrexian Ghoul before its own end-step sacrifice, and Mindslicer's death dumps hands when yours is already empty.

archetypes.pitch: A patient GW midrange plan that gets dramatically better once seven cards fill your graveyard. Cheap self-mill and cycling switch on huge threats like Mystic Enforcer and Werebear, and Glory shields your team from the yard. Rewarding if you like decks that quietly power up and then take over.
archetypes.rationale: Divine Sacrament, Mystic Enforcer, Werebear, Nantuko Monastery and friends all upgrade once "there are seven or more cards in your graveyard", and the cube's 20+ cycling cards plus Frantic Search/Millikin/Street Wraith fill the yard while replacing themselves; Glory grants color protection while sitting in the graveyard.

archetypes.pitch: A calm engine deck built on enchantments that draw you cards as you cast them. Mesa Enchantress and Zur the Enchanter bury opponents in card advantage while Sylvan Library and Mystic Remora refill your hand. For players who want to build a machine and win on sheer resources.
archetypes.rationale: Mesa Enchantress draws a card per enchantment cast and Zur the Enchanter puts any enchantment "with mana value 3 or less" straight onto the battlefield — Mystic Remora (1), Hunting Grounds (2), Sylvan Library (2), Divine Sacrament (3), Squirrel Nest (3); Sevinne's Reclamation and Auramancer rebuy them from the graveyard.

archetypes.pitch: Go wide with a green-white army and overwhelm the table. Saproling Symbiosis and Battle Screech flood the board, Divine Sacrament pumps the team, and Opposition can tap the opponent out of the game entirely. Perfect if you like big boards and swinging with everything.
archetypes.rationale: Opposition converts token width into a full tap-down lock; Saproling Symbiosis, Battle Screech, and Squirrel Nest go wide while Divine Sacrament pumps the white tokens, Congregate ("2 life for each creature") and Kavu Primarch's convoke cash the width in, and Nut Collector's threshold makes every Squirrel a 3/3.

archetypes.pitch: Skip the mana and drop game-ending monsters early. Entomb and Gamble load your graveyard, then Chainer and Dread Return bring the fatties back while Sneak Attack slams them from hand. For players who want explosive, do-something-huge turns.
archetypes.rationale: Entomb and Gamble (tutor plus random discard) stock the graveyard; Chainer, Dread Return, and Life // Death return the bodies while Sneak Attack cheats them in from hand; cross-tag: Worldly Tutor + Gamekeeper ("reveal cards from the top of your library until you reveal a creature card. Put that card onto the battlefield") cheats any creature from the library, and Arcanis, Denizen of the Deep, and Phantom Nishoba are untagged but textbook targets (huge bodies or a repeatable "{T}: Draw three cards").

archetypes.pitch: A UB tempo deck that profits from throwing cards away. Discard outlets like Aquamoeba and Zombie Infestation cast your madness spells at a discount, turning your bin into a weapon. Great for players who enjoy clever, cost-cutting sequencing.
archetypes.rationale: The four madness cards turn every discard outlet (Aquamoeba, Zombie Infestation, Jalum Tome, Vexing Sphinx's cumulative upkeep) into mana-discounted spells and Zombie tokens; a Mindslicer hand-dump is asymmetric when half your hand casts itself from exile.

archetypes.pitch: A smooth WR midrange deck that never floods because everything cycles. Lightning Rift and Invigorating Boon turn each cycled card into free damage or growth, so you always have something to do. Ideal for players who like consistency and incremental value.
archetypes.rationale: Lightning Rift and Invigorating Boon both trigger "whenever a player cycles a card" and the cube holds 20+ cyclers including five cycling lands; the same cycling doubles as Threshold fuel, cross-tag Jolrael converts each cycle draw into her "second card each turn" Cat trigger, and Grim Lavamancer ("Exile two cards from your graveyard") burns the spent cyclers.
archetypes.key_themes: Engine/Outlet payoffs on the cycling keyword; Graveyard cross-over

archetypes.pitch: A blue-red combo puzzle that ends the game in one big turn. High Tide and free untappers generate a mountain of mana, then Grapeshot or Empty the Warrens converts it into a kill. For players who love chaining spells toward a lethal finish.
archetypes.rationale: High Tide plus the free-untap suite (Turnabout, Frantic Search, Snap, Cloud of Faeries, Peregrine Drake) generates mana and storm count, Helm of Awakening discounts every spell, and Grapeshot / Empty the Warrens / Stroke of Genius convert the turn into a kill; Force of Will's alternative cost protects the combo turn while adding to storm, and Last Chance / Time Stretch buy the extra turn to finish.

archetypes.pitch: A WU tempo-value deck that reuses enter-the-battlefield effects over and over. Momentary Blink and Whitemane Lion re-trigger creatures like Flametongue Kavu and Man-o'-War to grind opponents out. Satisfying if you like value engines and answering everything.
archetypes.rationale: Momentary Blink, Whitemane Lion, and Sun Clasp rebuy enter-the-battlefield triggers (Flametongue Kavu, Man-o'-War, Phyrexian Rager, Deadwood Treefolk's "enters or leaves the battlefield" recursion); cross-tag Umbilicus — its upkeep bounce ("they return a permanent they control to its owner's hand") is pure upside when your permanents want to re-enter.

archetypes.pitch: A controlling WU lock-down deck that makes attacking you miserable. No Mercy and Windborn Muse punish aggression, Icy Manipulator taps threats, and Wrath of God resets the board before you close on card advantage. For players who enjoy saying no and winning slowly.
archetypes.rationale: No Mercy, Windborn Muse, Crawlspace, and Arboria make attacking miserable while Icy Manipulator and Nomad Decoy tap threats for cross-tag Royal Assassin ("Destroy target tapped creature"); Mystic Remora draws through it, Wrath of God resets, and Jester's Cap strips the opponent's win conditions in the attrition endgame.

archetypes.pitch: A blue artifact deck that turns trinkets into a mana and card engine. Urza, Lord High Artificer makes a giant Construct and mana from your artifacts, powering out big payoffs like Triskelion. For players who like combo-adjacent value engines.
archetypes.rationale: Urza's Construct token "gets +1/+1 for each artifact you control" and "Tap an untapped artifact you control: Add {U}" turns Mind Stone, Millikin, and even Ornithopter into mana; Urza's Blueprints' echo {6} is trivial with that mana, and Triskelion is the top-end sink Enlightened Tutor can find.

archetypes.pitch: A resilient white deck that turns a huge life total into a win condition. Test of Endurance and Serra Avatar cash in the life gained by Congregate, Lyra Dawnbringer, and Spirit Link. For players who like outlasting opponents and flipping defense into offense.
archetypes.rationale: Test of Endurance wins the game at 50 or more life and Serra Avatar's "power and toughness are each equal to your life total"; Congregate, Lyra's lifelink aura, Spirit Link, and Kjeldoran Gargoyle do the gaining, with Sol'kanar taxing every black spell for extra life.

archetypes.pitch: A GU ramp deck that makes every land drop pay off. Exploration and Tatyova, Benthic Druid turn extra lands into cards and life, while Terravore grows into a finisher off the graveyard. For players who enjoy accelerating ahead and grinding value.
archetypes.rationale: Exploration plus Tatyova turns every extra land drop into a card and a life; Terravore ("power and toughness are each equal to the number of land cards in all graveyards") feeds on the cube's cycling lands and Crop Rotation, while Kamahl and Squirrel Nest give flooded lands a job.

archetypes.pitch: A green counters deck that snowballs a single threat into a game-ender. Forgotten Ancient hoards counters and redistributes them onto Triskelion or the Phantoms, and proliferate keeps them flowing. For players who like building one unstoppable creature.
archetypes.rationale: Forgotten Ancient soaks a counter per spell and each upkeep may "move any number of +1/+1 counters from this creature onto other creatures" — onto Triskelion for direct damage or onto Phantom Flock / Phantom Nishoba to recharge their damage-prevention shields; Yawgmoth's proliferate and Dragon Blood keep the counters flowing.

archetypes.pitch: A build-around combo that makes a 20/20 flying indestructible token out of nowhere. Crop Rotation fetches Dark Depths and green ramp helps clear its ice counters for a sudden knockout. A high-risk, high-reward pick for players who love a flashy one-card haymaker.
archetypes.rationale: Dark Depths makes a legendary 20/20 flying indestructible token once its ten ice counters are gone; Crop Rotation ("Search your library for a land card, put that card onto the battlefield") fetches it, Exploration replays the land drops it eats, and Krosan Restorer's threshold untap helps pay the {3}-per-counter cost. Single-card anchor — speculate only with support.

archetypes.pitch: A greedy five-color goodstuff deck powered by heavy fixing. Lair lands, Gemstone Mine, and Birds of Paradise let you cast every gold bomb, with Legacy Weapon as a repeatable removal engine. For players who want to play the biggest, splashiest cards in the cube.
archetypes.rationale: Five Lair lands, Gemstone Mine, Lotus Blossom, and Birds of Paradise assemble WUBRG for the cube's gold top-end: Legacy Weapon's "{W}{U}{B}{R}{G}: Exile target permanent" becomes a repeatable removal engine, with Sol'kanar, Rith, Arcades Sabboth, and Xira Arien's card-draw sink as the payoffs the fixing earns.

archetypes.pitch: A single-color ramp deck that doubles your mana and dumps it into huge sinks. Gauntlet of Power supercharges your basics so firebreathers like Nantuko Shade and Shivan Dragon grow out of control. For players who like committing to one color and going tall.
archetypes.rationale: Gauntlet of Power pumps the chosen color and makes every basic of that color "add an additional one mana"; the cube is full of firebreathing-style sinks to spend it — Nantuko Shade and Shivan Dragon pump per mana, Howl from Beyond is an X-spell, and the Invokers carry 7-mana activations.

archetypes.pitch: A two-card blue engine that turns Horseshoe Crab into a machine gun. With Hermetic Study each untap is a ping, with Quicksilver Dagger it also draws a card, and with Opposition it locks down the board. A puzzle-piece build-around for players who love repeatable engines.
archetypes.rationale: Horseshoe Crab's "{U}: Untap this creature" repeats any tap ability: with Hermetic Study ("{T}: This creature deals 1 damage to any target") every {U} is a ping, with Quicksilver Dagger it is a ping plus a card, and with Opposition every {U} taps an opposing permanent. Two-card engine — draft the pieces together.

decks.identity: Mono-Black sacrifice midrange built around Yawgmoth, Oversold Cemetery, and recursive threats
decks.pitch: A grindy Mono-Black Aristocrats Midrange deck built around Yawgmoth, Thran Physician and Oversold Cemetery. The plan is to deploy cheap fodder, sacrifice it for value (Yawgmoth draws cards and removes threats; Phyrexian Ghoul grows; Dread Return reanimates), then recur the pieces with Oversold Cemetery and Necrosavant. Mindslicer provides a one-shot hand wipe once the opponent has more cards than you, and the removal suite keeps the board manageable while the engine comes online.

decks.identity: Mono-Black graveyard reanimator: Entomb/Zombie Infestation fill the yard, Dread Return/Life-Death/Chainer/Necrosavant/Body Snatcher cheat the payoffs into play. Worldgorger Dragon and Flametongue Kavu carry a Red identity but are reanimation-only and need zero Red sources.
decks.pitch: Macro-Archetype: Midrange (with a deliberate deviation). Projected Avg MV: 3.33. Land count 16 (40% of N=40) — at the top of Midrange's 38-42% band; this deck's activated abilities are colored-mana-hungry (Chainer BBB, Necrosavant 3BBB, Dread Return 2BB), so it wants to hit 4-6 lands reliably even though its actual curve is low. Threats/Payoffs sit at 9/24 non-land cards (37.5%, within the 30-40% Midrange band). Interaction/Disruption is 7/24 (29%, top of the 20-30% band). Infrastructure/Consistency (Entomb, Vampiric Tutor, Dread Return x2, Life//Death x2, Zombie Infestation x2 = 8/24, 33%) is called out as a deviation from Midrange's "0%, absorbed into threats" default — both self-grill agents independently confirmed this is warranted, not padding: Worldgorger Dragon and Necrosavant are functionally inert cards until the tutor-into-discard-into-reanimate chain resolves, so the enabling suite is genuine load-bearing infrastructure, not incidental value.

decks.strategy: Mono-Black removal-midrange with Gauntlet of Power big-mana payoffs (Nantuko Shade, Howl from Beyond) and a Zombie/sacrifice-value subtheme
decks.identity: Black removal-forward midrange leaning on Zombie/sacrifice value (Cackling Fiend, Necrosavant, Undead Gladiator, Zombie Infestation) with Nantuko Shade and Howl from Beyond converting Gauntlet of Power doubled Swamp mana into damage, Yawgmoth as a sacrifice-engine finisher, and Vampiric Tutor for consistency.
decks.pitch: This is a removal-dense black midrange deck built around a Zombie/sacrifice-value subtheme (Cackling Fiend, Necrosavant, Undead Gladiator, Zombie Infestation, Urborg Syphon-Mage) that grinds toward the midgame, where Nantuko Shade and Howl from Beyond convert Gauntlet of Power's doubled Swamp mana directly into damage. Yawgmoth, Thran Physician is the sacrifice-engine finisher, and Vampiric Tutor provides consistency by finding Gauntlet or whatever answer the matchup calls for.

decks.identity: Black-Green Aristocrats/Sacrifice midrange with a reanimator sub-package; Yawgmoth and Oversold Cemetery convert cheap fodder into removal, card draw, and recursion, while Entomb/Dread Return/Necrosavant cheat back threats.
decks.pitch: Cheap creatures die into sacrifice outlets (Phyrexian Ghoul, Yawgmoth, Phyrexian Debaser) for removal, pump, and card draw, while Oversold Cemetery rebuys the fodder once the graveyard fills up. Entomb, Dread Return, Gamekeeper, and Necrosavant give the deck a reanimator angle on top, letting it cheat Spiritmonger or loop Necrosavant back from the yard using the same fodder that feeds the sac outlets. Removal (Terror, Chainer's Edict, Faceless Butcher) and Mindslicer's symmetrical discard round out the interaction suite.

decks.identity: Black-Red Goblin tribal aggro that converts a wide token board into damage via sacrifice outlets, closing with burn.
decks.pitch: Macro-Archetype: Aggro. Projected Avg MV: 2.76.

decks.identity: Black-Red Goblin Tribal/Cheat with artifact cost reduction and creature cheat engines
decks.pitch: This deck's strongest draws involve Urza's Incubator on turn 2 followed by multiple cheap Goblins, or Cryptic Gateway on turn 5 tapping two Goblins to put Siege-Gang Commander directly into play. Dralnu's Crusade turns every Goblin into a 2/2 or larger threat and enables Gateway's shared-creature-type condition even more consistently.

decks.identity: Black-Red reanimator and sneak-attack cheat deck with big dragon payoffs
decks.pitch: Slot-allocation rationale. The deck is classified as Combo/Reanimator. Lands are 14 (35% of 40) — on the lean end, but four ramp pieces (Mind Stone x2, Millikin x2) effectively lower the curve and the audit accepts this as PASS. Engine & infrastructure density is high because every reanimation spell, tutor, discard outlet, and ramp piece is part of the combo chain. Payoff density is intentionally pushed above the baseline Combo range because Sneak Attack and Dread Return are dead without a creature target; Shivan Dragon, Macetail Hystrodon, Phyrexian Scuta, and Flametongue Kavu give enough bodies. Interaction is a competitive 5 cards: Duress protects the combo, Terror and Chainer's Edict clear blockers or hatebears.

decks.strategy: Sneak Attack / cheat big creatures reanimator
decks.identity: Black-Red reanimator that cheats oversized or high-value ETB creatures into play via Sneak Attack and a graveyard-recursion package (Chainer, Dread Return, Necrosavant), backed by Entomb and Vampiric Tutor for consistency.
decks.pitch: Curve and sequencing. The deck's real "combo" isn't two specific cards — it's a redundant web of enablers (Entomb, Zombie Infestation x2, Vampiric Tutor) feeding two independent cheat routes (Sneak Attack for hand-based haste, Chainer/Dread Return/Necrosavant for graveyard-based permanence). Curve: 2 one-drops, 7 two-drops, 4 three-drops, 8 four-drops (including Sneak Attack itself), 1 five-drop, 3 six-drops. Turn 4 is when the deck goes off: Sneak Attack, Dread Return, Faceless Butcher, and Flametongue Kavu are all live simultaneously, so a turn-1 Entomb into a turn-4 Dread Return or Sneak Attack activation is the deck's fastest clean line.

decks.identity: Black-Red grindy Aristocrats deck anchored on Yawgmoth, Thran Physician and Oversold Cemetery
decks.pitch: The engine loop. Yawgmoth needs bodies, and this deck has five distinct sacrifice outlets that can feed him for free or near-free (Phyrexian Ghoul x2, Phyrexian Debaser x2, Skirk Prospector x2, Necrosavant's own activation, Dread Return's flashback). 18 of the 24 nonland cards are creatures, so hitting Oversold Cemetery's four-creatures-in-graveyard threshold is easy through ordinary combat trades alone — the two discard outlets (Zombie Infestation, Urborg Syphon-Mage) accelerate it further by letting you post creatures to the yard directly from hand when flooded.

decks.strategy: BRG All-In Aristocrats (Yawgmoth sac-engine + goblin tribal + graveyard recursion)
decks.identity: Black-Red-Green synergy midrange: Yawgmoth converts fodder into cards and removal, Oversold Cemetery/Dread Return/Necrosavant rebuy the fodder, Siege-Gang Commander/Flametongue Kavu close games.
decks.pitch: Yawgmoth converts every death in the deck into a card and a -1/-1 counter; Mogg War Marshal, Zombie Infestation, Festering Goblin, and Penumbra Bobcat exist purely to feed him and Skirk Prospector/Necrosavant. Oversold Cemetery and Dread Return rebuy the fodder once four-plus creatures are in the yard, and Siege-Gang Commander/Flametongue Kavu turn removal and tokens into a closing burst of reach.

decks.identity: Red-Green cycling-payoff shell splashing Black for free-to-cycle cards; Lightning Rift and Invigorating Boon trigger off any cycled card, Jolrael converts the extra draw into Cat tokens, Grim Lavamancer burns the spent cyclers.
decks.pitch: The engine, quantified. 21 of 25 mainboard spells carry Cycling/Forestcycling. Every cycle activation is a trigger for both Lightning Rift (pay {1}, 2 damage to anything) and Invigorating Boon (free +1/+1 counter) simultaneously - meaning a single cycled Street Wraith on turn 3 can read "pay 2 life, draw a card, deal 2 damage, put a counter on a creature" for one activation. This compounds fast: by turn 5-6 with both enchantments live, every spare cycler in hand is doing double duty as both card filtering and a value trigger.

decks.strategy: BRG Tutor-Toolbox Reanimator / Cheat Big Creatures
decks.identity: Black-Red core with a light Green splash; two 1-mana tutors and Entomb assemble the graveyard, Dread Return/Life-Death/Necrosavant/Sneak Attack/Gamekeeper each independently cheat a huge creature into play.
decks.pitch: Vampiric Tutor and Worldly Tutor find whatever piece is missing; Entomb instantly stocks the graveyard with Worldgorger Dragon or Spiritmonger for Dread Return / Life//Death / Necrosavant to reanimate. Sneak Attack cheats creatures straight from hand, and the signature toolbox line — Worldly Tutor sets a creature on top of the library, then Phyrexian Ghoul sacrifices Gamekeeper to reveal-and-cheat that exact card into play for free — ties the whole shell together. Five precious rare/mythic slots go entirely to engine pieces (two tutors, Entomb, Sneak Attack, Worldgorger Dragon); every big body backing them up is a common or uncommon.

decks.identity: Yawgmoth/Oversold Cemetery sac-recursion engine backed by BW removal (Swords to Plowshares, Terror, Chainer's Edict, Wrath of God), with Lieutenant Kirtar and Mindslicer as supporting keystones and Battle Screech/Zombie Infestation/Undead Gladiator sustaining fodder density.
decks.pitch: Yawgmoth, Thran Physician and Oversold Cemetery form the engine: every cheap creature that trades or dies becomes free removal, a card, and eventually a rebought threat. Lieutenant Kirtar and Wrath of God give the deck real answers so it can survive to the mid-game, while Mindslicer turns a naturally-emptying hand into a one-sided Wheel of Fate against the opponent. Battle Screech, Zombie Infestation, and Undead Gladiator keep the sac-fodder supply from running dry, and Necrosavant provides a recursive finisher for games that go long.

decks.strategy: Colorless Artifacts Affinity (Aggro/Midrange) with a light single-blue splash
decks.identity: Mono-colorless artifact curve-out deck (Ornithopter/Millikin/Wall of Junk into Juggernaut/Dodecapod/Dragon Engine, closing with Triskelion), with a deliberately light 5-card blue splash of single-pip commons added to fill a pool-depth shortfall under the rarity restrictions.
decks.pitch: This is a mono-colorless Artifacts curve-out deck with a deliberately light 5-card blue splash (all single-U-pip commons) added to solve a hard pool-depth shortfall — the cube's pure-colorless card pool (23 unique cards) can't fill a 40+10 build under the stated rarity restrictions on its own. Ornithopter/Millikin/Wall of Junk hold the early turns, Juggernaut/Dodecapod/Dragon Engine carry the midgame, and Triskelion closes as a repeatable-removal finisher. Urza's Incubator discounts the deck's three Construct creatures by {2} each, while Icy Manipulator and Mind Stone/Jalum Tome supply interaction and card flow.

decks.identity: Mono-Green midrange with zero fixing risk; Forgotten Ancient/Triskelion/Kavu Primarch/Invigorating Boon/Dragon Blood counters package backed by generic ramp, card advantage, and curve threats.
decks.pitch: Be clear-eyed about what this deck actually is. Only 6 of the 24 nonland cards genuinely place, move, or spend +1/+1 counters: Forgotten Ancient, Triskelion, Kavu Primarch x2, and Dragon Blood x2. This is fewer synergy pieces than the sibling GB and GW builds (which run 8-9 apiece), because mono-G/colorless is the smallest legal slice of the cube's already-thin 12-card counters pool. The self-grill was blunt about this: it's honestly closer to "green goodstuff midrange with a counters garnish" than a tight synergy deck. If you want the strongest expression of the counters theme, the GB or GW build will feel more like a build-around; pick this one specifically for its zero-fixing-risk mana base and generically solid curve.

decks.strategy: Green ramp midrange with Dark Depths as top-end insurance
decks.identity: Mono-Green ramp/midrange deck that wins through combat pressure and card advantage, with Dark Depths as a bonus late-game win condition rather than the sole plan.
decks.pitch: Green has no removal in this cube -- verified twice. Both grill agents independently scanned the full 462-entry pool for any green card with destroy/fight/-X/-X/damage-to-creature text and found zero. This shapes the whole build: Giant Spider and Maze of Ith aren't "nice to have," they're the only two answers to an evasive or must-kill threat that exist in the color at all.

decks.strategy: Dark Depths turbo combo (mono-G, light B splash)
decks.identity: Mono-Green combo deck built to tutor, ramp toward, and protect Dark Depths, with a single-card Black splash for Vampiric Tutor.
decks.pitch: Mana math for the combo: Dark Depths needs 30 total mana ({3}x10) spread over the game, plus 1 land sacrificed to Crop Rotation. With Krosan Restorer's threshold ability (untap up to 3 lands) and Wild Growth (+1 extra G per tap), a 15-land base functionally produces well above its raw count once the graveyard fills. Threshold (7+ cards in graveyard) is reachable via Crop Rotation's sacrifice, Lull's cycling, Emerald Charm's cycling-adjacent flexibility, and normal attrition -- Werebear and Krosan Restorer both key off it.

decks.strategy: Mono-Green ramp deck accelerating toward Kamahl Fist of Krosa and Stonewood Invoker as Gauntlet of Power-fueled mana sinks, with Sylvan Library and Exploration for consistency
decks.identity: Green ramp (Birds of Paradise, Werebear, Wild Growth, Nature's Lore, Krosan Restorer) accelerating to Kamahl Fist of Krosa's repeatable land-animation anthem and Stonewood Invoker's 7-mana firebreathing, with Gauntlet of Power doubling Forest mana (and stacking with Wild Growth for triple production off one land) and Sylvan Library/Exploration providing consistency.
decks.pitch: A genuine ramp deck — Birds of Paradise, Werebear x2, Wild Growth x2, Nature's Lore, and Krosan Restorer accelerate toward Kamahl, Fist of Krosa (a repeatable land-animation anthem) and Stonewood Invoker (a literal 7-mana firebreathing sink), with Exploration adding extra land drops and Sylvan Library providing card advantage to smooth the climb. The manabase is 15 basic Forests with zero nonbasics, to maximize Gauntlet of Power's basic-land trigger.

decks.identity: Mono-green Lands-Matter token swarm ramping into Squirrel Nest and Kamahl overrun
decks.pitch: Macro-Archetype: Midrange | Projected Avg MV: 2.6

decks.identity: Black-Green midrange built around Yawgmoth's proliferate ability feeding Forgotten Ancient and Triskelion, with cheap sacrifice fodder keeping Yawgmoth's outlet fed.
decks.pitch: How the engine actually works. Yawgmoth is the sole proliferate source in the entire 271-card cube -- there is no redundancy for it. When it resolves, its `{B}{B}, discard a card: Proliferate` line adds counters to *every* permanent already carrying one: it grows Forgotten Ancient (more counters to redistribute at upkeep), tops up Triskelion for another ping, and advances Phyrexian Scuta/Kavu Primarch. Forgotten Ancient's upkeep trigger is the actual redistribution engine even without Yawgmoth in play -- it accrues a counter off *any* player's spell and can dump the pile onto Triskelion for a burst of direct damage, which is the core "soak and release" pattern from the original archetype brief.

decks.identity: Ramp every extra land drop into cards via Tatyova, Benthic Druid, then close with Kamahl, Fist of Krosa animating and pumping the team.
decks.pitch: Ramp every extra land drop into a card via Tatyova, Benthic Druid, then close the game with Kamahl, Fist of Krosa animating and pumping the team (including any Squirrel Nest tokens). Exploration, Nature's Lore, Wild Growth, and Crop Rotation accelerate past curve while Sylvan Library and Fa'adiyah Seer keep the hand full of gas. Terravore rides along as a secondary beater that grows for free off cycling lands and Crop Rotation's sacrifice. Counterspell, Man-o'-War, and Snap give just enough GU tempo to protect the plan.

decks.identity: Feed lands into every graveyard on the table to grow Terravore fast, backed by cheap efficient bodies and a tight GU tempo suite.
decks.pitch: Feed lands into every graveyard on the table -- cycling lands, Terminal Moraine's sacrifice, and Crop Rotation's sac cost all convert a land directly into Terravore's power and toughness -- while cheap efficient bodies and a tight GU tempo suite (Counterspell, Man-o'-War, Snap, Ovinize) keep the board and clock in your favor. Invigorating Boon turns every cycle (yours or the opponent's) into a free +1/+1 counter, and Jolrael/Squirrel Nest convert spare card draws and lands into extra bodies.

decks.identity: Low-curve GW beatdown that fills the graveyard via a native cycling package to flip a cluster of Threshold creatures into a lethal board, backed by Divine Sacrament.
decks.pitch: A low-curve GW beatdown deck that races opponents while its native cycling package (Drifting Meadow, Slippery Karst, Fa'adiyah Seer, Radiant's Judgment) fills the graveyard toward the Threshold line of 7+ cards. Once online, a cluster of cheap Threshold creatures (Werebear, Mystic Zealot, Mystic Enforcer, Vigilant Sentry, Nomad Decoy, Battlefield Scrounger, Nantuko Monastery) all upgrade simultaneously, turning an already-aggressive board into a lethal one, backed by Divine Sacrament's white anthem.

decks.identity: Green-White token swarm using recurring token engines (Squirrel Nest, flashback Battle Screech/Call of the Herd), an anthem (Divine Sacrament), and mass-token payoffs (Saproling Symbiosis, Jolrael, Nut Collector) to close via combat damage, Kavu Primarch convoke, or Congregate life gain.
decks.pitch: A green-white token swarm that wins by going wide faster than the opponent can answer it. Squirrel Nest, flashback Battle Screech, and flashback Call of the Herd generate a stream of cheap bodies; Divine Sacrament and Saproling Symbiosis convert that width into real damage, while Jolrael and Nut Collector keep refilling the board turn after turn. Kavu Primarch cashes the width in directly via convoke, and Congregate turns an unblocked board into a life-total blowout. A lean removal suite (Swords to Plowshares, Pacifism, Radiant's Judgment) buys the time needed to assemble the swarm, with Enlightened Tutor smoothing draws toward the key payoff enchantments.

decks.identity: Green-White midrange built around Phantom Nishoba/Phantom Flock's damage-prevention shields, recharged by Forgotten Ancient and Dragon Blood, backed by premium removal and token generation.
decks.pitch: How the shields actually recharge. Phantom Flock and Phantom Nishoba both read "if damage would be dealt to this creature, prevent that damage. Remove a +1/+1 counter from this creature" -- each counter is a one-time damage-prevention charge, not a permanent ability. Forgotten Ancient's upkeep trigger ("move any number of +1/+1 counters from this creature onto other creatures") is the fastest way to top them back up, and Dragon Blood's `{3},{T}: put a +1/+1 counter on target creature` is the reliable, mana-gated backup that doesn't depend on anything else happening first. Between the two, a Nishoba or Flock can realistically survive more than one combat per game -- but neither engine is fast, so expect to play defense (removal, Pacifism, Whitemane Lion tempo plays) while the recharge sources come online.

decks.identity: GW Midrange built around Hunting Grounds cheating creatures into play once Threshold (7+ graveyard cards) is active; Threshold payoffs scale up across the curve, fueled by a native GW cycling package.
decks.pitch: Macro-Archetype: Midrange. Projected Avg MV: 3.12.

decks.identity: Mono-Red Goblins swarming with disposable tokens, cashed in via Pashalik Mons and Siege-Gang Commander, closed out with efficient burn and Sulfuric Vortex.
decks.pitch: Goblin tutor correction: Goblin Matron can only fetch cards with the Goblin creature type -- Skirk Prospector, Mogg War Marshal, Subterranean Scout, Gempalm Incinerator, Goblin Medics, Pashalik Mons, Siege-Gang Commander, or the second Matron. It cannot fetch Sulfuric Vortex (an Enchantment, not a Goblin card) -- plan Matron activations accordingly.

decks.strategy: Mono-Red Goblin aggro with Gauntlet of Power big-mana firebreathing payoffs (Dragon Whelp, Avarax, Shivan Dragon) and a Sneak Attack cheat-into-play package
decks.identity: Red Goblin tribal aggro (Skirk Prospector, Mogg War Marshal, Goblin Matron, Siege-Gang Commander, Pashalik Mons) that functions independently of its payoffs, with Gauntlet of Power doubling Mountain mana to fuel Dragon Whelp/Avarax/Shivan Dragon firebreathing and Sneak Attack cheating dragons into play for free.
decks.pitch: A red Goblin-tribal shell that plays a real aggressive game plan on its own — Skirk Prospector, Mogg War Marshal, and Goblin Matron curve into Siege-Gang Commander and Pashalik Mons for sacrifice-fueled reach — with Gauntlet of Power as a mythic bonus that doubles every Mountain's output and turns Dragon Whelp, Avarax, and Shivan Dragon's repeatable firebreathing abilities into game-ending mana sinks. Sneak Attack is the explosive top-end: for {R} it cheats Shivan Dragon into play with haste, sidestepping the mana cost entirely. The manabase is 16 basic Mountains with zero nonbasics by design, since Gauntlet's bonus only triggers off basic lands.

decks.identity: Red-Black Goblins aristocrats: Pashalik Mons and Skirk Prospector convert Goblin deaths into damage/mana, Dralnu's Crusade + Deadapult provide repeatable reach, Urza's Incubator discounts the curve.
decks.pitch: Pashalik Mons and Skirk Prospector turn every dying Goblin into damage or mana, while Dralnu's Crusade makes the whole tribe black Zombies so Deadapult can eat any of them for reach. Urza's Incubator discounts the Goblin curve (Siege-Gang Commander down to {1}{R}{R}), and Sulfuric Vortex plus a burn suite close the game even if the fragile 1-2 toughness bodies trade off in combat.

decks.identity: Red-Green Cycling burn deck: Lightning Rift and Invigorating Boon convert every cycle (yours or the opponents) into incremental damage or +1/+1 counters, backed by an efficient burn suite and Grim Lavamancer/Jolrael as graveyard/card-advantage payoffs.
decks.pitch: Color correction. The archetype brief this deck was built from claimed "WR" as the color identity, but that was wrong: Invigorating Boon's oracle text confirms it is Green ("Whenever a player cycles a card, you may put a +1/+1 counter on target creature"), not White or Red. Cross-checking every suggested core card against its actual `colors` field showed the true keystone pair — Lightning Rift (R) and Invigorating Boon (G) — sits in Gruul, and Gruul also holds the deepest well of on-color cyclers in the pool (6 Green, 5 Red, versus 3 White, 3 Black, 2 Blue). The deck was built RG on that basis, confirmed with the user before construction.

decks.strategy: Cycling payoffs (Lightning Rift / Invigorating Boon) in RG midrange, light W splash
decks.identity: RG Cycling midrange with a light White removal splash; Lightning Rift and Invigorating Boon convert every cycle into damage or board growth
decks.pitch: Every cycler in this deck is a two-mode card: draw a card now, or hold it as a threat/trick for later — and either way it triggers Lightning Rift (2 damage) and Invigorating Boon (+1/+1 counter) on the way past. Jolrael turns a second cycle-draw each turn into a 2/2 Cat, Grim Lavamancer turns the graveyard those discards pile into repeatable burn, and Werebear turns the same graveyard into a 5/5 mana dork. Birds of Paradise and three W duals carry a light two-spell White splash (Swords to Plowshares, Radiant's Judgment) without diluting the RG core.

decks.identity: Red-Green Goblin tribal go-wide aggro: cheap Goblins and token doublers flood the board, Pashalik Mons and Siege-Gang Commander convert Goblin deaths into reach, Kavu Primarch cashes in board width via convoke.
decks.pitch: A Goblin-tribal go-wide plan: cheap Goblins (Mogg War Marshal, Skirk Prospector) and token-doublers (Squirrel Nest, Saproling Symbiosis) flood the board, Pashalik Mons and Siege-Gang Commander turn dying/sacrificed Goblins into direct damage, and Kavu Primarch converts the leftover width into a free-or-cheap convoked threat. Interaction (Chain Lightning, Flametongue Kavu, Gempalm Incinerator, Solar Blast) keeps the attack lane clear while the deck races.

decks.strategy: Mono-U tempo/control with Horseshoe Crab + Opposition as a late-game tap-down lock, High Tide as a mana-doubling accelerant, backed by hard countermagic, tempo bounce, and Arcanis the Omnipotent as a real finisher
decks.identity: Mono-U tempo/control lock deck
decks.pitch: The engine, honestly assessed. Horseshoe Crab ("{U}: Untap this creature") plus Opposition ("Tap an untapped creature you control: Tap target artifact, creature, or land") is a real two-card interaction: enchant nothing, just tap the Crab to satisfy Opposition's cost, then pay {U} to untap the Crab and repeat — every spare blue mana becomes one more tapped-down opposing permanent. But the self-grill on this exact question (independently run twice) concluded the same thing both times: with only 1 Opposition and 2 Horseshoe Crabs in 40 cards, this is a low-frequency bonus, not a load-bearing win condition. Opposition alone already taps one permanent per turn using *any* untapped creature you control (not just the Crab), and Icy Manipulator gives a mana-costed version of the same effect that needs no creature at all. Play the deck as a mono-U tempo/control shell first; treat the full Crab lock as a ceiling-raiser when it comes together, not the plan you're drawing toward.

decks.identity: Mono-Blue control shell built around Urza, Lord High Artificer, using a colorless artifact mana-rock/threat package to power the Construct token and blue interaction to protect the plan.
decks.pitch: Mono-Blue control shell built around Urza, Lord High Artificer -- a keystone that turns every artifact into a mana source and produces a Construct token that scales with your artifact count. A dense colorless artifact package (mana rocks, cheap fodder, mid-curve beaters) fuels both the token and Urza's own tap ability, while a real blue interaction suite (Counterspell, Force of Will, tempo bounce) protects the plan and buys time for Urza's Blueprints and Stroke of Genius to grind out the win. Triskelion is the top-end finisher/removal sink.

decks.strategy: Graveyard Grind - recursive value engine using discard outlets and madness spells
decks.identity: Blue-Black graveyard grind with discard-to-value engine, Urborg Syphon-Mage life drain, and Zombie token pressure
decks.pitch: Lands: 17 (42.5% of N=40) -- Midrange wants 38-42%; 17 reflects the deck's need to hit 3 mana for engine deployment while running cantrips and Frantic Search's virtual mana.

decks.strategy: UB Madness / discard-value with a light Reanimator sub-package, R splash for Gamble
decks.identity: UB Madness-Reanimator hybrid: four Madness cards discounted via 8 discard outlets, feeding a recursion package (Body Snatcher, Chainer Dementia Master, Dread Return) and grindy payoffs (Vexing Sphinx, Mindslicer, Urborg Syphon-Mage).
decks.pitch: Madness math. 4 Madness cards, 8 real discard outlets (Aquamoeba, Zombie Infestation x2, Jalum Tome, Frantic Search, Vexing Sphinx's cumulative upkeep, Body Snatcher's ETB, Gamble's forced discard), plus 2 cyclers in the sideboard swap pool. On the play, a hand with any Madness card and any outlet routinely turns a 6-mana Dark Withering into a 1-mana Terror-with-upside, or an Obsessive Search into a free cantrip regardless of which half of the trigger you take.

decks.identity: Control-midrange grind built around Vexing Sphinx, Mindslicer, and Circular Logic, converting a deep discard-outlet package into madness value, tokens, and drain
decks.pitch: Macro-Archetype: Midrange (control-leaning). Projected Avg MV: 2.75 (matches mana audit exactly).

decks.strategy: GU Balanced Hybrid (all four Lands-Matter payoffs)
decks.identity: Runs Tatyova, Kamahl, Terravore, and Squirrel Nest as co-equal payoffs sharing one pool of ramp and fixing, trading focus for resilience.
decks.pitch: All four Lands-Matter payoffs run as co-equal pieces of one shared engine: every land drop from Exploration, Nature's Lore, Crop Rotation, and Terminal Moraine simultaneously triggers Tatyova's draw, feeds Kamahl's mana, gives Squirrel Nest another target, and (via Crop Rotation/Terminal Moraine's sacrifice) fuels Terravore's graveyard count. No single payoff gets a dedicated support package -- instead, one pool of ramp/fixing/card-selection cashes in on whichever payoff draws well that game.

decks.strategy: Mono-U control with a light R splash, running all three payoffs (Hermetic Study, Opposition, Quicksilver Dagger x2) for maximum engine redundancy, plus High Tide as a mana-doubling accelerant
decks.identity: Mono-U control, triple-payoff redundancy build
decks.pitch: This deck tests a real hypothesis: does running all three payoffs actually help? The self-grill answered mostly no, and it's worth stating plainly rather than dressing it up. Opposition and Hermetic Study/Quicksilver Dagger want opposite creature states — Opposition needs the Crab *untapped* to pay its cost, the Auras need the Crab *tapped* to fire their ability — so drawing multiple payoffs together doesn't stack, it competes for the same scarce resource (a live, uninterrupted Crab). Auras are also a real liability the standalone effects don't share: kill the enchanted Crab and the Aura dies with it, a two-for-one Opposition and Icy Manipulator are immune to. The honest framing is: this deck runs three *ways in* to the same basic plan (spend spare {U} to do something extra), not three stacking layers of power.

decks.strategy: UR tempo-burn with Horseshoe Crab + Hermetic Study/Quicksilver Dagger as a repeatable damage engine, backed by a real R burn suite
decks.identity: UR tempo-burn deck
decks.pitch: Two engines, not one. Horseshoe Crab pairs with Hermetic Study (any target) and Quicksilver Dagger (face + draw a card) — since both are single-target Auras, at most one is ever active on a given Crab at once, so running both isn't additive redundancy so much as insurance against one copy getting removed or stuck in hand. The self-grill flagged the original 2/2 split (2x Hermetic Study, 2x Quicksilver Dagger) as over-built relative to what the combo actually needs; this build trims to 1x Hermetic Study (freeing a slot for Mind Stone) while keeping Quicksilver Dagger at 2 copies, since Dagger is the card that actually needs the R splash to matter and losing a copy of it would make the R investment harder to justify.

decks.identity: UR Storm/High Tide combo — chains free-untap effects and cost reduction into a lethal Grapeshot/Empty the Warrens storm turn
decks.pitch: The mana math: with High Tide active, the 12 Island-typed sources (10 Island + 2 Molten Tributary) can produce up to 24 U from lands alone before a single untap effect resolves. Turnabout and Peregrine Drake then re-tap that same land base, so a clean draw can chain Obsessive Search into High Tide into Cloud of Faeries/Peregrine Drake into Turnabout into Grapeshot for lethal well before the deck runs out of gas. Helm of Awakening compounds this by shaving 1 off every spell in the chain (including the opponent's, which is a real, accepted symmetry cost).

decks.strategy: High Tide combo with a control-leaning card-advantage backbone
decks.identity: Blue-Red High Tide combo: doubles Island mana, chains free-untap spells for storm count and card advantage, kills via Grapeshot or Empty the Warrens into Last Chance.
decks.pitch: The kill lines. Two distinct finishers exist because this pool has no "win on its own" storm payoff (no Tendrils of Agony analog): 1. Grapeshot for reach/direct damage, scaling with storm count. 2. Empty the Warrens into Last Chance -- the tokens summoning-sick this turn are NOT sick on the bonus turn Last Chance grants (no opposing turn intervenes), so this is a legal, reliable attack for lethal even without a huge Grapeshot storm count. This line is more consistent than raw Grapeshot damage.

decks.identity: Blue-Red tempo shell (cheap interaction, card selection, efficient bodies) layered with a High Tide/storm combo backup plan (Grapeshot, Empty the Warrens) protected by Force of Will and Overmaster
decks.pitch: Slot allocation. Macro-Archetype: Tempo (with Combo overlay). Lands 15/40 = 37.5% — modestly below the generic constructed baseline (16), justified by 5 mana-neutral untap effects (Cloud of Faeries x2, Snap x2, Frantic Search x2, Peregrine Drake, Turnabout) acting as pseudo-lands, plus Helm of Awakening's blanket discount. Of the 25 nonland cards: ~9 Interaction (Counterspell, Snap, Fire//Ice, Grim Lavamancer, Gempalm Incinerator, Force of Will), ~7 Payoffs/Threats (Grapeshot, Empty the Warrens, Storm Entity, Peregrine Drake), ~9 Engine/Infrastructure (High Tide, Turnabout, Helm of Awakening, Mystical Tutor, Overmaster, Frantic Search, Cloud of Faeries) — a Tempo/Combo-hybrid spread, roughly matching the 25-35% Interaction / 10-18% Payoff / 20-30% Engine bands for Tempo with Combo's Engine weighting pulled up.

decks.identity: White-Blue control shell that wins by not dying: Test of Endurance (50+ life) and Serra Avatar (P/T = life total) as win conditions, backed by Wrath of God, Counterspell, Absorb and Swords to Plowshares for interaction, with Congregate, Cleric of the Forward Order, Lyra Dawnbringer and Spirit Link doing the lifegain.
decks.pitch: The math on the win conditions. Test of Endurance triggers at the *beginning of your upkeep* with 50+ life — it does not win the turn you cross the threshold if you gain life during your opponent's turn or in response to something; you need to start your own turn already at 50+. Starting life is 20; you need +30. Congregate alone can supply a big chunk of that against a populated board (2 life per creature *on the battlefield*, including the opponent's), and Lyra/Kjeldoran-style damage-into-life plus Spirit Link on a repeatedly-connecting creature are the realistic grind path. Serra Avatar is the more reliable win condition in practice — it doesn't need a specific threshold, just a life total high enough to out-power whatever's on the other side of the board, and its "shuffle into library on death" clause means removal-based answers just delay it, they don't 2-for-1 it.

decks.strategy: mono-white lifegain combo-control (Test of Endurance / Serra Avatar alt-win)
decks.identity: Mono-White combo-control stacking redundant lifegain (Lyra Dawnbringer, Kjeldoran Gargoyle, Spirit Link, Cleric of the Forward Order, Congregate) behind real interaction (Wrath of God, Swords to Plowshares, Pacifism, Icy Manipulator) to enable Test of Endurance (win at 50+ life) or a massive Serra Avatar.
decks.pitch: The math on Test of Endurance. Starting at 20 life, you need +30. Direct sources: Congregate (2 per creature on the battlefield -- with just 4-5 bodies out that's 8-10 in one shot, twice), Renewed Faith (6), Cleric of the Forward Order (2, or 4 with both copies down). Repeatable sources: Kjeldoran Gargoyle and Lyra both gain life equal to combat damage dealt every single hit; Spirit Link turns any creature -- including a chump-blocked attacker or an opposing creature you've bounced control of -- into the same engine. In practice the deck rarely "goes off"; it just accumulates until either wincon is live almost as a side effect of playing normal Magic.

decks.identity: White-Black lifegain/drain control that wins via Test of Endurance (50+ life) or a maxed-out Serra Avatar
decks.pitch: The lifegain math. Over a full game this deck can plausibly generate: Renewed Faith x2 (~+12), Congregate x2 (~+8-16, scales off *all* creatures on the battlefield, not just yours), Cleric of the Forward Order x2 (+4-6), Gerrard's Verdict (+0-6), repeated Urborg Syphon-Mage activations (+2 per activation), and ongoing Lyra Dawnbringer/Kjeldoran Gargoyle combat lifelink. That comfortably closes the 30-life gap from a starting 20 to Test of Endurance's 50 threshold if even half of it lands.

decks.identity: White-Green enchantment-engine midrange: Mesa Enchantress and Sylvan Library convert enchantment casts and draw-step selection into card advantage, Auramancer/Sevinne's Reclamation/tutors keep the engine running, Divine Sacrament closes with a white-creature anthem.
decks.pitch: Engine math. 13 of the 40 cards are enchantment-type spells (Sylvan Library, Divine Sacrament, Squirrel Nest x2, Seton's Desire x2, Griffin Guide, Wild Growth x2, Spirit Link, Pacifism x2, Sun Clasp) — every one of them draws a card off Mesa Enchantress on cast. Auramancer (x2) is the only card that turns a resolved enchantment back into a fresh cast trigger; Sevinne's Reclamation reanimates a permanent directly onto the battlefield and does not re-trigger Mesa Enchantress, despite being a recursion piece. Realistic expectation: 2-4 Mesa Enchantress triggers per game once it's online, not a continuous chain — this is a grindy value/midrange shell, not a true storm-style engine.

decks.strategy: WG Enchantress engine + Zur (BUW splash) toolbox
decks.identity: White-Green Enchantress value-engine midrange, splashing U/B for Zur the Enchanter as a tutor-cheat payoff
decks.pitch: Mesa Enchantress and Sylvan Library turn every enchantment you cast into a card, while Squirrel Nest and Wild Growth's auras keep the trigger firing cheaply. Zur the Enchanter is the payoff on top: attack once and pull any mana-value-3-or-less enchantment straight onto the battlefield — Sylvan Library, Squirrel Nest, or a Pacifism to answer a blocker. Auramancer and Sevinne's Reclamation loop the whole package back out of the graveyard, so losing a permanent to removal rarely sticks.

decks.identity: White-Red Aura-Voltron Aggro built around Valduk, Keeper of the Flame, backed by an Enchantress card-draw/recursion core
decks.pitch: A small, resilient suite of buff Auras (Griffin Guide, Undying Rage, Lightning Reflexes) either turns Valduk, Keeper of the Flame into a token-generating engine or makes an evasive White beater (Voice of All, Serra Angel, Ridgetop Raptor) into a real clock. An "Enchantress" card-advantage core backs the plan: Mesa Enchantress draws off every enchantment cast, while Auramancer and Tiana rebuy dead Auras from the graveyard, and Enlightened Tutor / Sevinne's Reclamation find or rebuy whatever piece is missing. Lyra Dawnbringer tops the curve as a lifelink closer that quietly anthems the deck's other three Angels.

decks.strategy: Naya (GWR) go-wide tokens, cash-in via Kavu Primarch convoke / Congregate / Kamahl overrun, closed by Rith the Awakener
decks.identity: Naya go-wide tokens with efficient removal and a color-agnostic overrun finisher
decks.pitch: Slot allocation. Macro-Archetype: Midrange. Projected Avg MV: 3.17. Lands: 16 (40% of N=40) — standard for 3-color Midrange with a CMC6 top end. Interaction: 7 (29% of 24 nonland) — within the 20-30% Midrange band. Threats/Payoffs: 17 (71% of nonland) — deviates well above the stated 30-40% guidance; justified because the Engine/Infra budget is deliberately absorbed into this bucket, since nearly every token generator here (Battle Screech, Squirrel Nest, Mogg War Marshal, Saproling Symbiosis) is simultaneously its own value engine. No ramp/cantrip modifiers applied (ramp_count=0, no cantrips in the 40), so the land count stays at the unmodified baseline.

decks.strategy: Naya Aura-Voltron Aggro (Valduk, Keeper of the Flame)
decks.identity: Naya beatdown stacking resilient combat Auras onto efficient creatures, with Valduk converting attached Auras into extra hasty attackers each combat; functions as a normal aggro deck even without Valduk live.
decks.pitch: Macro-Archetype: Aggro. Projected Avg MV: 2.60 (nonland).

decks.identity: White-Blue tempo-value shell built around repeatable ETB triggers
decks.pitch: A WU tempo-value shell built entirely around repeatable "enters the battlefield" triggers. Whitemane Lion, Momentary Blink, Sun Clasp, and Sawtooth Loon all exist to rebuy Man-o'-War (tempo removal), Cloud of Faeries / Peregrine Drake (mana untap, effectively free spells), and each other. Umbilicus turns that loop into a free, symmetric-but-net-positive engine every single upkeep. There's no single "win condition" card — the payoff is cumulative tempo and card advantage, backed by real WU interaction (Swords to Plowshares, Counterspell, Absorb, Pacifism) so the deck can survive long enough to grind the opponent out. Serra Angel is the lone dedicated closer once the engine has taken over the game.

decks.identity: WU Opposition tap-lock control with a light B splash for Royal Assassin
decks.pitch: Slot allocation. Lands: 17 (42.5% of N=40) — control decks with a 4-mana engine centerpiece (Opposition) and a 4-mana sweeper (Wrath) want to hit land drops reliably; sits at the low end of the 42-47% Control range. Of the 23 non-land cards: Interaction 13 (56.5%), Engine/Infra 8 (34.8%), Threats/Payoffs 2 (8.7%). Interaction and Engine both run well above the typical Control reference ranges (35-45% / 10-20%) — this is a deliberate deviation, not an oversight: Icy Manipulator, Nomad Decoy, and Royal Assassin are simultaneously the deck's interaction (they answer threats) and its engine (they feed and enable Opposition), so classifying them into one bucket inflates that bucket at the other's expense. The real cost of this shape is thin top-end — only 2 dedicated finishers — which is accepted here because Opposition itself is a slow-burning win condition (denying the opponent all their permanents eventually ends the game on its own), not because the deck has genuine card-advantage insurance to spare.

decks.identity: WU control that stacks redundant attack-tax/stax effects (Windborn Muse, Crawlspace, Damping Sphere, Mystic Remora, Icy Manipulator) over conventional removal, counterspells, and a Wrath of God reset, closing with evasive fliers.
decks.pitch: Every threat the opponent plays gets more expensive to swing with, and every swing that does happen is capped and punished. Windborn Muse and Crawlspace stack independent attack taxes — pay {2} per attacker, and cap at two attackers regardless — while Wall of Junk and Floodgate hold the fort as recastable/self-punishing blockers. Damping Sphere and Mystic Remora extend the tax plan to spells themselves, generating card advantage in the process. Icy Manipulator locks down whatever gets through, Wrath of God resets bad boards, and Counterspell/Absorb protect the plan until Serra Angel or Voice of All close it out in the air.

decks.identity: White-Blue-Black ETB-value midrange: cheap enters-the-battlefield creatures rebought by blink/bounce effects for grinding card and tempo advantage, backed by a board wipe and premium removal.
decks.pitch: Self-grill resolution. Two independent agents (Proposer/Challenger) reviewed this list against the full working pool. The Challenger's one must-fix was a mislabeled role on Body Snatcher — its ETB is a *cost* (discard a creature or it's exiled), not removal; the trigger that actually returns value is its death trigger (reanimates the discarded creature). The role above is corrected. Practically, this means Body Snatcher plays best as a one-time value piece — cast it once for the discard/reanimate sequence — rather than a repeat blink target, since rebuying it via Momentary Blink or Umbilicus costs you a card each time instead of generating one. The Challenger also flagged that 16 lands with avg CMC 2.92 and no true ramp is slightly greedy for a 3-color 40-card deck; the automated audit still PASSes at 16, so it's left as-is, but if games feel mana-hungry in practice, cutting Serra Angel for a 17th land is the cleanest adjustment. The sideboard's original build skewed 4-of-10 toward control/combo answers with no aggro-specific removal; Terror replaces the second Duress to cover that gap.

decks.strategy: Prison / Stax Control — No Mercy Hard Lockdown
decks.identity: WU prison control with a light B splash for No Mercy; wins by making combat unprofitable (chump blocks, taps, fogs) and punishing any creature that connects, then closing with evasive card-advantage threats.
decks.pitch: The interaction-to-threat ratio is deliberately extreme, and that's the point. 17 of 23 nonland cards (74%) are pure interaction/prison pieces — well above the 35-45% Control reference range. That's not an oversight: in a "make attacking miserable" prison shell, the interaction *is* the win condition. Only Serra Angel and Thieving Magpie exist purely to close games; everything else exists to make sure the opponent never gets to play Magic. This is a deliberate deviation from the Control baseline, not an error.

decks.strategy: Five-color (WUBRG) legendary midrange — one 3-color legend per wedge, curve-out to Rith/Sol'kanar/Arcades
decks.identity: WUBRG midrange built entirely around 5 three-color legends (Xira Arien, Zur, Sol'kanar, Rith, Arcades Sabboth), each touching every color exactly 3 times; fixing from Lair lands and common duals only, no any-color rares.
decks.pitch: All five colors are touched by exactly 3 of the 5 legends — a deliberate structural mirror of the 5 Lair lands, which are each tri-color and also touch every color exactly 3 times. This symmetry is why the manabase (6 sources per color, before basics) lines up so cleanly with 4 of the 5 payoffs.

decks.strategy: Five-color (WUBRG) midrange-control hybrid — Legacy Weapon's engine plus a 3-legend curve (Zur/Sol'kanar/Rith)
decks.identity: WUBRG midrange-control hybrid splitting the rare budget between Legacy Weapon's repeatable exile engine and 3 curve-topping legends (Zur, Sol'kanar, Rith), backed by Birds of Paradise and common/uncommon 5-color fixing.
decks.pitch: This build deliberately cuts Arcades Sabboth, Xira Arien, Gemstone Mine, and Lotus Blossom to keep 3 legends (Zur/Sol'kanar/Rith) alongside Legacy Weapon and Birds of Paradise. Compared to the other two decks from this cube, it trades Five Wedge Legends' Xira Arien (cheap, low-risk) and Arcades Sabboth (near-unplayable in that build) for Legacy Weapon's grinding removal engine, and trades Legacy Weapon Control's Gemstone Mine/Lotus Blossom "any-color" redundancy for two more curve-topping threats.

decks.strategy: Five-color (WUBRG) control built around Legacy Weapon's repeatable exile activation
decks.identity: WUBRG control: hard interaction + card advantage backstopped by Legacy Weapon's repeatable exile, closed out by evasive threats (Zur, Serra Angel, Thieving Magpie) enhanced by cheap auras.
decks.pitch: Legacy Weapon is a removal engine, not the win condition. It has no power/toughness — it clears the way while Zur, Serra Angel, Thieving Magpie, or a Griffin-Guided body actually closes the game. Framing it purely as a "win condition" (as an early draft of this deck's role text did) overstates what it does; the self-grill caught this.
